# The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Basics of obstetrics and gynecology > The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac*

[Original Article Link](/library/Do01VS)

---

## Summary

The <u>placenta</u>, <u>umbilical cord</u>, and <u>amniotic sac</u> protect and provide <u>nutrients</u> to the fetus. The <u>placenta</u> is a fetomaternal organ that enables the selective transfer of <u>nutrients</u> and gases between mother and fetus. The <u>placental barrier</u> limits direct contact between the embryo and maternal blood, thus protecting both mother and child from potentially harmful substances (e.g., blood cell <u>antigens</u> of the unborn, bacteria from the mother). In addition, the <u>placenta</u> produces <u>hormones</u> that mediate maternal adaptation to <u>pregnancy</u> and maintain <u>pregnancy</u>. Establishing <u>uteroplacental circulation</u> involves several steps, including endovascular <u>trophoblast</u> invasion and uterine vascular remodeling. The 50–70 centimeter long <u>umbilical cord</u> connects the <u>placenta</u> with the fetus and contains one <u>umbilical vein</u> that carries oxygenated, <u>nutrient</u>-rich blood supply and two <u>umbilical arteries</u> that carry deoxygenated blood from fetus to the <u>placenta</u> and the maternal circulation. The <u>amniotic sac</u> surrounds the fetus and contains the <u>amniotic fluid</u>, providing mechanical protection to the developing fetus.

---

## Development of uteroplacental circulation

Following implantation of the egg, the <u>endometrial</u> stromal cell lining is transformed into the <u>decidua</u> (<u>decidual reaction</u>). The <u>decidua</u> provides nourishment to the conceptus until the definitive <u>placenta</u> forms. Approximately on day 12 of <u>embryonic development</u>, fetal <u>blood vessels</u> come into contact with maternal blood through openings in maternal vessels, forming a region of fetal-maternal exchange.




### Decidual reaction




* <u>Decidual reaction</u>:  (<u>decidualization</u>): implantation → thickening and structural changes of the <u>endometrium</u> → formation of <u>decidua</u>

* Function of <u>decidua</u>

* Histiotrophic nutrition 

* Storage of fat and <u>glycogen</u> causes <u>endometrial</u> cell enlargement

* Secretion of lytic enzymes by the <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u> during invasion of the <u>decidua</u> → <u>nutrient</u> uptake by the <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u>

* <u>Immune privilege</u>: <u>tight junctions</u> separate the conceptus from adjacent <u>endometrial</u> tissue

* Preparation for <u>placental</u> circulation: increased <u>progesterone</u> → transformation of decidual vessels into a network of <u>anastomosing</u> <u>spiral arteries</u> (uterine vascular remodeling)

* The decidua has three distinct parts, distinguished by their relation to the site of implantation:

* Decidua basalis: maternal portion of the <u>placenta</u>

* Decidua capsularis: <u>decidua</u> that grows over the <u>blastocyst</u> after implantation, appearing as a cap-like structure

* Decidua parietalis: <u>decidua</u> lining the <u>uterus</u> elsewhere than at the site of implantation





### Placentation




<u>Placentation</u> refers to the development of the <u>placenta</u>. The embryonic portion of the <u>placenta</u> is derived from cells of the <u>trophoblast</u> and the maternal portion of the <u>decidua basalis</u>.




* Early <u>placental development</u>

* Prelacunar stage: until approx. day 9 of <u>embryonic development</u>

* Lacunar stage

* From approx. day 9 of <u>embryogenesis</u>

* Lacunae form in <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u>, these are separated by thin <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u> trabeculae

* Lytic enzymes of <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u> eventually erode the <u>spiral arteries</u> of the <u>decidua</u>, and maternal blood fills the lacunae.

* Lacunae merge to form the <u>intervillous space</u>.

* Hemotrophic nutrition: <u>nutrient</u> supply from maternal blood  [[1]](/library/-zbDvw)

* Early villous stage: from approx. day 13–28 of <u>embryogenesis</u>

* Chorionic villi development and maturation: the composition of <u>chorionic villi</u> changes during the course of <u>placental development</u>. 

* Primary villi

* Develop through migration of <u>cytotrophoblast</u> cells into the <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u> trabeculae

* Structure

* Inner layer: <u>cytotrophoblasts</u>

* Outer layer: <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u> cells with <u>microvilli</u>

* Secondary villi

* Develop through migration of extraembryonic <u>mesoderm</u> cells into the center of <u>primary villi</u>

* Structure

* <u>Mesenchymal</u> core

* Inner layer: <u>cytotrophoblast</u>

* Outer layer: <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u> cells with <u>microvilli</u>

* Tertiary villi (<u>terminal villi</u>): connect to the <u>umbilical cord</u> vessels during week 3 of <u>embryonic development</u>

* <u>Tertiary villi</u> develop through vascularization

* <u>Terminal villi</u> develop after the 4<sup>th</sup> month → <u>cytotrophoblast</u> cells begin to disappear → with only isolated <u>cytotrophoblast</u> cells (Langhans cells ) remaining

* Structure of <u>terminal villi</u>

* <u>Mesenchymal</u> core with fetal <u>capillaries</u>

* Inner layer: Langhans cells (isolated <u>cytotrophoblast</u> cells)

* Outer layer: <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u>

## The placenta

### <u>Placental</u> structure




At term, the mature <u>placenta</u> weighs approx. 500 g, is about 2 cm thick, and has a diameter of 15–20 cm. It consists of three parts:




* <u>Basal plate</u> (<u>decidua basalis</u>): mainly maternal component

* <u>Intervillous space</u> and <u>villous trees</u>: fetomaternal zone

* <u>Chorionic plate</u>: fetal component





![Macroscopic structure of the placenta](media/ofvb26hwfmqg7dvxwmn04e76.jpg)

Macroscopic structure of the placenta




#### Basal plate (placenta)




* Description: mainly maternal component, abuts the uterine wall

* Structure: maternal <u>decidua</u> with invading embryonal cells (<u>cytotrophoblast</u>, <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u>, and extravillous <u>trophoblast</u> cells)

* Blood supply: : uterine <u>spiral arteries</u>

* Placental septa: protrude at several sites in the <u>intervillous space</u>

* Placental cotyledons: 15–30 separations of the <u>decidua basalis</u>, formed by the <u>placental septa</u>, that can macroscopically be distinguished from each other





#### <u>Intervillous space</u> and <u>villous trees</u>




* Intervillous space

* Contact zone between maternal and fetal <u>placental</u> structures (site of fetomaternal gas and <u>nutrient</u> exchange)

* Filled with maternal blood

* Contains protruding <u>villous trees</u>

* Villous trees: The <u>placenta</u> is composed of 30–50 branching <u>villous trees</u>. 

* Stem villi: basal region of <u>villous trees</u> with fetal <u>arteries</u> and <u>veins</u>

* Intermediate villi: region of <u>villous trees</u> with fetal <u>arterioles</u>, <u>venules</u>, and <u>capillaries</u>; important region of gas and <u>nutrient</u> exchange

* Terminal villi: <u>tertiary villi</u> that float freely in the <u>intervillous space</u> and are directly involved in gas and <u>nutrient</u> exchange

* Anchoring villi: anchor the <u>villous trees</u> to the <u>decidua</u>
* The <u>cytotrophoblast</u> of <u>anchoring villi</u> expands and positions itself between the <u>decidua</u> and the <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u>.





#### Chorionic plate




* Description: : Fetal component of the <u>placenta</u>

* Structure: formed by the <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u>, the <u>cytotrophoblast</u>, and the somatic layer of the extraembryonic <u>mesoderm</u>

* Chorion frondosum: contains villi, is involved in the formation of the <u>placenta</u>

* Chorion laeve: outer layer of the fetal <u>placenta</u>, does not contain villi (not involved in the formation of the <u>placenta</u>)

### Placental barrier




Maternal and <u>fetal circulation</u> are separated by the <u>placental barrier</u>. The <u>placental barrier</u> controls the gas and <u>nutrient</u> exchange. Until the fourth month of development, the <u>placental barrier</u> consists of six layers. After the fourth month, the <u>cytotrophoblast</u> disappears from the villous wall, leaving only the isolated <u>cytotrophoblast</u> cells (Langhans cells).




* Structure until the 4<sup>th</sup> month of <u>embryonic development</u> (from maternal to fetal)
1. * <u>Syncytiotrophoblast</u>
2. * <u>Cytotrophoblast</u>
3. * <u>Basal lamina</u> of <u>trophoblasts</u>
4. * Villous stroma made up of <u>connective tissue</u>
5. * <u>Basal lamina</u> of the <u>endothelium</u>
6. * <u>Capillary</u> <u>endothelium</u>

* Structure from the 4<sup>th</sup> month of <u>embryonic development</u> (from maternal to fetal)
1. * <u>Syncytiotrophoblast</u>
2. * Fused <u>basal lamina</u> from <u>trophoblasts</u> and the <u>endothelium</u>
3. * <u>Capillary</u> <u>endothelium</u>





![Structure of the placental barrier](media/h98ftbf92d3hj4dw7ckg1aso.jpg)

Structure of the placental barrier




> [!TIP]
> After <u>birth</u>, the <u>placenta</u> must be inspected to ensure it has detached completely from the uterine wall. If this does not occur, there is a risk of <u>postpartum hemorrhage</u>. The check is performed by inspecting for the completeness of all <u>placental cotyledons</u>. On the fetal side, the <u>placenta</u> should be covered by the <u>amnion</u>.

## Placental function

### Overview of <u>placental</u> <u>hormones</u>




The most important <u>placental</u> <u>hormones</u> are <u>HCG</u>, <u>HPL</u>, <u>CRH</u>, <u>estrogen</u>, and <u>progesterone</u>; other important <u>hormones</u> during <u>pregnancy</u> include <u>thyroid hormones</u>, <u>oxytocin</u>, and <u>prolactin</u>.




* Site of production: <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u>

* Function of <u>hormones</u>

* Continuation of <u>pregnancy</u>

* Maternal adaptation to the <u>pregnancy</u>

* Regulation of uterine circulation

* <u>Fetal development</u> and growth

* Inducing <u>labor</u>





#### <u>Hormones</u> and the <u>placenta</u>

### Gas and <u>nutrient</u> exchange




The <u>placenta</u> is the main site of metabolites and <u>gas exchange</u> between the mother and the fetus.




* Passive transport

* <u>Diffusion</u>: O<sub>2</sub>;  , CO<sub>2</sub>, <u>creatinine</u>, <u>urea</u>, <u>bilirubin</u>, water, drugs

* <u>Facilitated diffusion</u>: <u>glucose</u>, <u>lactate</u>

* <u>Active transport</u>: <u>amino acids</u>, <u>peptides</u>, <u>hormones</u>, <u>vitamins</u>, <u>fatty acids</u>, inorganic ions
* <u>Pinocytosis</u>: <u>proteins</u>, lipids, <u>antibodies</u> (<u>IgG</u>)





![Placental gas and nutrient exchange](media/x75hverct4kkaq2ug4a1pc9h.jpg)

Placental gas and nutrient exchange




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Fat-soluble vitamins</u> (A, D, E, K), <u>immunoglobulins</u> (except <u>IgG</u>), and most <u>proteins</u> are either unable to cross the <u>placental barrier</u> or have only limited ability to do so. <u>Vitamin K</u> is an important <u>cofactor</u> for blood coagulation and should be administered to <u>the newborn infant</u> directly after <u>birth</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Anti-D</u> <u>antibodies</u> from the Rhesus system (<u>IgG antibodies</u>) are able to cross the <u>placental barrier</u>. In contrast, isoagglutinins of the ABO system are mainly <u>IgM antibodies</u>, which cannot cross the <u>placental barrier</u>!

## The umbilical cord

The <u>umbilical cord</u> connects the fetus with the fetal part of the <u>placenta</u> (<u>chorionic plate</u>). It typically attaches centrally to the <u>chorionic plate</u> of the <u>placenta</u>. The development of the <u>umbilical cord</u> begins at approx. the 3<sup>rd</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>. By the end of <u>pregnancy</u>, the <u>umbilical cord</u> is approx. 50–70 cm long.









### Formation and structure of the <u>umbilical cord</u>



* The <u>umbilical cord</u> contains 3 <u>allantois</u>-derived <u>blood vessels</u> that carry fetal blood: 

* 2 umbilical arteries: branches from the <u>internal iliac arteries</u> that carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the <u>placenta</u>

* 1 umbilical vein: supplies oxygenated, <u>nutrient</u>-rich blood from the <u>placenta</u> to the fetus (merges into the <u>inferior vena cava</u> via the <u>ductus venosus</u>)




#### Structure and development of the <u>umbilical cord</u> during early <u>pregnancy</u>




* Connecting stalk: precursor of the <u>umbilical cord</u>

* Content

* <u>Allantois</u>

* Small sac-like structure that forms the <u>yolk sac</u> and protrudes into the <u>connecting stalk</u> during the 3<sup>rd</sup> week of development

* The fetal <u>bladder</u> develops at the transition from the <u>allantoic</u> <u>epithelium</u> to the <u>endoderm</u> of the <u>hindgut</u>.

* Vitelline duct

* Connects the <u>midgut</u> to the <u>yolk sac</u>

* Obliterates during  6–7<sup>th</sup> week

* Failure to fully obliterate can lead to the following conditions

* No obliteration (patent <u>vitelline duct</u>): vitelline fistula (presents with <u>meconium</u> discharge from the <u>umbilicus</u> after <u>birth</u>)

* Partial obliteration: vitelline cyst (a cystic remnant which can lead to <u>small bowel obstruction</u> if bowel twists around the cyst) or <u>Meckel diverticulum</u>





#### Structure of the <u>umbilical cord</u> during late <u>pregnancy</u>




* <u>ECM</u>: <u>Wharton jelly</u> (gelatinous <u>connective tissue</u>)

* Cover: amniotic <u>epithelium</u>

* Content:

* <u>Urachus</u> (duct between fetal <u>bladder</u> and <u>umbilicus</u>)

* Remnant of the <u>allantois</u>

* Obliterates after <u>birth</u> to form the <u>median umbilical ligament</u>, covered by the <u>median umbilical fold</u> of the <u>peritoneum</u>

* Failure to involute may lead to anomalies with an increased risk of <u>malignancy</u> (<u>urachal</u> cancer) and infection.

* Remnants of the obliterated <u>vitelline duct</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>umbilical arteries</u> carry deoxygenated blood, whereas the <u>umbilical vein</u> carries oxygenated blood!




> [!TIP]
> A single <u>umbilical artery</u> is a sign of <u>chromosomal</u> disease and congenital anomalies. [[2]](/library/iObJHF)

### Physiological <u>umbilical hernia</u>




Due to the rapid growth of the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>, there is not enough space within the embryonic <u>abdominal cavity</u> from the 6<sup>th</sup> to the 10<sup>th</sup> week of development. As a result, sections of the gut herniate into the <u>extraembryonic coelom</u> of the future <u>umbilical cord</u> during this time.

---

## Amnion and amniotic cavity

### Amniotic cavity




The <u>amniotic sac</u> is formed very early in <u>pregnancy</u> and surrounds the embryo as a protective shell. As the fetus grows, the <u>amniotic cavity</u> expands, eventually resulting in the displacement of the <u>chorionic cavity</u> and the <u>uterine cavity</u>.




* Development: 2<sup>nd</sup> week of development through migration of <u>epiblast</u> cells

* Components

* Lined with amniotic <u>epithelial</u> cells

* Filled with <u>amniotic fluid</u>, which is produced by amniotic <u>epithelial</u> cells





#### Amniotic sac




The <u>amniotic sac</u> is composed of maternal (<u>decidua</u>) and fetal components (chorioamniotic membranes) that surround the fetus and provide mechanical protection.




* <u>Amnion</u>

* Inner <u>amniotic membrane</u>

* Develops from the <u>embryoblast</u>

* Secretes <u>amniotic fluid</u>

* Chorion

* Middle <u>amniotic membrane</u>

* Develops from the <u>cytotrophoblast</u>

* <u>Decidua</u>

* Outermost membrane

* Develops from the <u>decidua capsularis</u>, which lies above the site of implantation





#### Amniotic fluid




Protective fluid within the <u>amniotic sac</u> that cushions the fetus, prevents adherence of the fetus to the <u>amnion</u>, and serves as a transport medium for <u>nutrients</u> and metabolites.




* Composition: initially a clear liquid 

* Amount: approx. 850–1500 mL by the end of <u>pregnancy</u> (the <u>amniotic fluid</u> is completely exchanged every 3 hours)

* <u>pH</u>: 7–7.5 (slightly alkaline)

* <u>Proteins</u>, <u>glucose</u>, <u>urea</u>

* Fetal urine, <u>lung</u> fluids, <u>hair</u>, dead <u>skin</u>, <u>sebum</u>

* Vernix: a milky-white, lipid-rich substance that consists of fetal <u>dermal</u> cells and <u>sebaceous gland</u> secretions. It covers the fetus's <u>skin</u> (especially in the <u>third trimester</u>).

* Reabsorption  

* Reabsorption by the amniotic <u>epithelium</u>

* The fetus swallows approx. 400 mL of <u>amniotic fluid</u> per day, which is excreted through the <u>kidneys</u>.
